title: Bells
hookLine: bells call to prayer, toll for death, ring for joy

lines: NOON: A BELL OVER THE ROOFTOPS.
cards: Noon in a small town. A bell rings out over the rooftops. Nobody sent a text, but a woman in a shop doorway glances up, and an old man lowers his newspaper.
Another day, the same bell rings slowly: one stroke, then a long gap, then another. People on the street go quiet, because they know what that means. Someone has died.
And another day, every bell in the tower goes at once, and a wedding party spills into the sunlight. One tower, three messages, and the whole town reads them without a word.

teach.h: GOLDEN BELLS ON THE PRIEST'S ROBE.
teach.b: Church bells do three jobs. Start with Exodus, where the high priest's robe has golden bells along its hem, between pomegranates of colored thread. Why bells?
"His sound shall be heard when he goeth in unto the holy place before the LORD." A bell announces that someone is coming before God, and a church bell carries a sound like that out to a whole town.

First job: the call to prayer. In Catholic tradition, the Angelus bell rings at set hours of the day, and people stop and pray where they are. Orthodox ringers strike patterns for the services and feasts.
Second job: the toll for death, a slow bell for someone who has died.

teach.h: A TOLL: IT TOLLS FOR THEE.
teach.b: The poet and preacher John Donne, lying sick and hearing a church bell toll for someone else, wrote that we should never send to ask who it's for, because it tolls for us as well: "never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee."
In Donne's reading, this death belongs to all of us. Third job: joy. Weddings.
In Catholic churches, the bells fall silent on Holy Thursday and come back ringing at the Easter Vigil.
The prophet Zechariah even pictures a day when holiness reaches the ordinary bells: "In that day shall there be upon the bells of the horses, HOLINESS UNTO THE LORD."
Put the three together and you hear Paul: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." A bell does both, out loud, for everyone in earshot.

how: Churches ring bells to call people to services and to prayer, toll them slowly at funerals, and ring them in celebration at weddings and feasts; in Catholic tradition the Angelus bell rings at set hours, and the bells fall silent from Holy Thursday until the Easter Vigil.

games.q: you hear a church bell tolling slowly, one stroke and a long gap. John Donne has advice. what is it?
o: send someone to find out who died
don't ask who it's for: it tolls for you too
close the window and carry on
games.why: "never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee." in Donne's view, every death belongs to everyone.

practice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable, and listen outward, past the room, for anything that rings or chimes, a clock, a bike, a spoon against a glass, or whatever is farthest away.
If you pray, hold one person in mind for each sound you hear. When the bell comes at the end, let it ring all the way out before you move.

wordCard.voice: Bells. A church tower's voice: they call to prayer, toll for the dead, and ring for joy, so a whole town hears.

orig.note: Hebrew: bell, the word for the golden bells on the high priest's robe in Exodus 28.

carryVoice: Your line: for whom it tolls. Joy and grief, rung out for everyone. Until tomorrow.
